text.p: Lithuanian newspapers carried the following reports in their editions on Saturday, which today is a working day. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy:

- The growing crime rate and more frequent attacks against the church and its servants is frightening priests. Younger priests no longer want to "turn the other cheek" and are buying weapons to defend themselves.

- Three emigre Lithuanians, colonels in the U.S. Army, have been offered posts in the new government. They helped draw up plans for the state's defence and now their main task is to create an effective force that will meet NATO standards.
- Reminders of Christmas in Vilnius are scarce, apart from a good trade in Christmas trees.

- President Algirdas Brazauskas vetoed two laws on public servants and work contracts which would introduce a special qualification process for employees, which if they failed could lead to them being sacked.
- Former prime minister Aleksandras Abisala refused an offer to work as a special ambassador for contacts with European nations.

- A Lithuanian-American joint venture was the only company to offer to administrate the proposed free economic zone in the northern town of Siauliai. The company, Siauliai skrydis, is part owned by the U.S.-based Baltic Fund, Britain's Lazard Brothers and the Saudi Al-Ibrahim family.
- Gazprom and Lithuania signed a deal for three billion cubic metres of natural gas in 1997.
- The newspaper has an interview with popular Latvian composer Raimond Pauls, who will have to combine his activities with those of his work in the president's office.
